::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
A complete commercial location study, in R and in Python side by side. You will predict how many people walk past every candidate location in central Sydney, turn footfall into an audience score for three kinds of advertiser, and rank the bus shelters, banners and bus routes an advertiser can actually buy. Along the way you will meet the two mistakes that make most published footfall models look better than they are.
:::

## The question an advertiser asks

Out-of-home (OOH) advertising is everything a person sees outside their own home: billboards, bus shelters, street banners, the sides of buses. Unlike online advertising, it cannot count its own audience. A website knows who loaded a page; a bus shelter does not know who walked past it. The price of a site, and the advertiser's decision to buy it, therefore rest on an estimate of who is there.

That estimate has three parts, and this chapter builds each in turn.

1. **Footfall.** How many people pass the location? This is a prediction problem: a few dozen locations are counted, and every other location has to be inferred from what surrounds it.
2. **Audience.** Are they the right people? A bank and a fast-food chain want different audiences from the same footfall. This is a weighting problem, and the weights are a judgement.
3. **Inventory.** Which of the places that can be bought reach that audience? This is a spatial join of the scores onto the bus shelters, banners and routes that are for sale.

The chapter is written in both R and Python. The analysis was first built in R with `caret`, which remains common in consultancy and in applied statistics, and every listing has a Python twin that does the same thing with `scikit-learn` and `geopandas`. Read whichever you work in; the reasoning is the same.

## The data

Every input is open, and one script rebuilds all of them, so the whole study can be rerun from nothing.

| Input | Source | How it is used |
|---|---|---|
| Walking counts | City of Sydney walking count surveys, 2022–2023 | Target: mean weekday count of the three post-COVID surveys at each site |
| Points of interest, fast food, education, finance | OpenStreetMap | Kernel density surfaces (quartic, 250 m radius) |
| Roads, bus stops and stations | OpenStreetMap | Road length and stop density surfaces |
| Building surface and volume | GHSL P2023A, 2020 (Earth Engine) | Built-up surface and volume per 100 m cell |
| Night-time light | VIIRS annual composite, 2022 (Earth Engine) | Average radiance |
| Jobs and floor space | City of Sydney floor space and employment survey, 2022 | Jobs per hectare by block, nearest block attributes |
| Household income | ABS Census 2021, G02, by SA2 | Median weekly household income |
| Population by age | WorldPop 2020, 100 m, age and sex (Earth Engine) | Summed per SA2 into the advertisers' age bands |
| Bus shelters, banners | City of Sydney open data | The inventory to be scored |
| Bus routes | OpenStreetMap route relations | The inventory to be scored |
| Candidate locations | A point every 100 m along the street network | Where footfall is predicted |

{{< include _snippets/ch65_ooh_data.qmd >}}

The training target is the City of Sydney's walking counts. Twice a year the City counts pedestrians at around 100 locations from 6 am to midnight, on a weekday and a weekend day, in autumn and spring. The model predicts the mean weekday count of the three surveys after the COVID-19 restrictions ended (autumn 2022, spring 2022 and autumn 2023), available at 115 of the 120 sites. Counts run from 256 to 72,352 people a day, with a median of 6,080.

The predictors describe what surrounds each location: density surfaces of points of interest, road length and public-transport stops, built-up surface and volume, night-time light, job density, and the jobs, floor space and businesses of the nearest employment-survey block. That last join has a trap of its own. Count sites stand on streets, and streets lie between survey blocks, so a 'point in polygon' join matches almost nothing; the scripts take the nearest block instead.

## Building the features at three scales

A pedestrian count depends on what is on the street and on what is in the neighbourhood. A shop on the corner draws people; so does the station 600 metres away that sends them past the corner. Every surface is therefore summarised three times, as the mean within 100, 500 and 1000 metres of the location.

Two details matter. The buffers must be in metres, so the data must be in a projected coordinate system in metres, such as MGA zone 56 for Sydney; both scripts stop if they are not. And the mean is area-weighted (`exactextract`), so a pixel half inside a buffer counts half, which matters at 100 m where a buffer covers only a few dozen pixels.

## Look before you model

Before any model is fitted, two intermediate results are worth reading (both appear under the code below). The first is the maps of the seven surfaces with the counted sites on top, which show at a glance that footfall, night-time light, jobs and building volume all peak on the same CBD spine, and that the count sites sample that spine densely and the residential south thinly.

The second is the correlation of every surface with the count at each buffer size. Night-time light, job density, building volume and points of interest all correlate at about 0.7 to 0.8 with weekday footfall. Bus stops matter at 500 m but much less at 100 m: a stop draws people along the street towards it, not only to the kerb beside it. Built-up surface barely correlates at all, and slightly negatively at 1000 m, because the suburbs are full of houses that cover the ground but send few people onto the street. Two surfaces that sound alike (building surface and building volume) carry opposite information, which is the reason to look before modelling.

One scale effect is easy to miss. The VIIRS night-light pixel is about 500 m across, so its "100 m" mean is really the value of a single pixel, not a measurement of the street.

## The two mistakes, and how the scripts avoid them

### The test set that was used for training

A common pattern, and the one in the first version of this analysis, takes a 20 per cent sample of the data, fits the pre-processing on that sample (centring, scaling, Box–Cox), and then uses the same sample as the test set. The model is never trained on those rows, so it looks like a fair test. It is not quite: the test rows have shaped the transformation every training row went through. A second, larger version of the same leak is to report R² on all the counted sites, training sites included, because that number measures memory as much as prediction.

The scripts hold out 20 per cent of the counted sites first, before anything is learned, and put the pre-processing inside each model so that it is refitted in every fold. The only number reported as performance is on the held-out sites.

### The neighbour in the training fold

Count sites in a city centre are a few hundred metres apart. Two sites on the same street share their 500 m and 1000 m buffers almost entirely. Under ordinary random cross-validation, a validation site usually has a near-twin in the training fold, and the model is rewarded for interpolating between neighbours, which it will not be able to do at a genuinely new location.

The scripts compare random folds with spatial folds, in which the training sites are grouped into five location clusters and each cluster is held out in turn.

For every learner, spatial folds give an error 31 to 56 per cent larger than random folds (table below the code). A random split would have reported an error a third to a half smaller than the model will make on a street it has not seen. The ranking of the learners also changes less than their errors do: Cubist and boosted trees are best under both schemes.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
When the sites you validate on sit next to the sites you train on, a random split measures how well the model interpolates, not how well it predicts. Ask where the model will be used. If it will be used between the training sites, random folds are fine. If it will be used on new streets, suburbs or cities, validate on held-out places.
:::

## Six learners and a stack

The target is modelled on a log scale. Counts span more than two orders of magnitude, and a model fitted on raw counts spends its whole effort on the ten busiest CBD corners: in a first run on raw counts, the held-out MAPE exceeded 130 per cent because quiet streets were predicted at several times their true count. Fitting log(1 + count) and transforming back puts a laneway and a CBD corner on comparable terms.

Six models with different inductive biases are tuned by random search: an elastic net (`glmnet` / `ElasticNet`), a random forest (`ranger` / `RandomForestRegressor`), Cubist rule-based regression, a linear support vector machine, gradient-boosted trees (`xgboost` in Python; `gbm` in R, because caret's `xgbTree` no longer works with xgboost 3) and a small neural network. A stack then learns how to combine their predictions: Cubist is the meta-learner in Python, and an elastic net in R, where a Cubist meta-learner over all six models crashed `caretStack` in testing.

Stacking helps only when the base models make different mistakes, so the R script prints the correlation between their resampled errors before stacking. Highly correlated learners add little.

{{< include _snippets/ch65_ooh_sydney.qmd >}}

On the 23 held-out sites, the best single learners explain 82 to 88 per cent of the variance in weekday counts, with an RMSE of about 4,400 to 5,200 people a day. The stack does not beat them here: its RMSE of 4,900 is in the middle of the pack, because its base learners make very similar mistakes and 92 training sites leave the meta-learner little to learn from. The percentage error remains high, around 80 to 100 per cent, and it is driven by the quietest sites, where predicting 900 people for a street that saw 300 is a large relative miss and a small absolute one. For an advertiser that asymmetry is acceptable, since it is the busy sites that are bought, but it should be stated. The R version draws its own random 20 per cent (24 sites) and uses `gbm` for boosting; its stack reaches R² 0.70 on those sites. The difference is a reminder of how much a held-out score from two dozen sites depends on which two dozen they are. Both versions choose the same best bus route for every advertiser.

Permutation importance on the held-out sites shows what the stack relies on: night-time light and points of interest immediately around the site, then road density and points of interest within 500 m, then the floor-space ratio of the nearest block. The model reads footfall from what is on the street first and from the neighbourhood second, which is what a planner walking the city would expect.

## From footfall to audience

Footfall is not an audience. A multi-criteria score combines the predicted count with weekly household income, population, the population in an age band, and the density of related businesses within 500 m, each rescaled to 0–1:

| Advertiser | Income + population | Footfall | Related businesses | Age band |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Financial services | 0.50 | 0.20 | 0.20 (financial) | 0.10 (40–64) |
| Fast food | 0.15 | 0.40 | 0.35 (fast food) | 0.10 (15–44) |
| Education | 0.05 | 0.20 | 0.35 (education) | 0.40 (20–34) |

These weights are a media planner's judgement, not a measurement. They are written down so that a client can disagree with one and see what changes, which is the same argument made for the SHAP-derived weights in Chapter [-@sec-vector].

## From audience to inventory

An advertiser cannot buy a scored point; it buys a bus shelter, a banner or a route. Each shelter and banner takes the mean score of the scored locations within 50 m. Each bus route takes the mean score of the scored locations it passes.

The mean matters. The first version of this analysis summed the scores along each route, which ranks routes largely by their length: a long route passes more locations and collects more score whether or not its audience is better. The scripts report the mean per location, with route length beside it, so that a planner can trade audience quality against reach explicitly.

Footfall is predicted at 6,202 candidate street locations, every 100 m along the network. The map shows the pattern each weighting produces. Fast food concentrates on the CBD spine and Haymarket, where footfall carries 40 per cent of the weight. Education peaks around Ultimo, Chippendale and the universities, where young adults live and education points of interest cluster. Financial services spread into the wealthier residential suburbs, because income and population carry half of that score.

A route needs at least five scored locations before its mean is ranked, which removes routes that merely clip the edge of the city.

## What the model is not

It predicts weekday counts from 6 am to midnight in fair weather, at the scale of the counted sites. It knows nothing of events, school holidays, construction or which side of the street a shelter faces. The OpenStreetMap layers are downloaded for the City of Sydney only, so the 1000 m buffers of sites near the boundary see fewer shops and roads than are really there, and footfall near the edge is likely to be underestimated. The MCDA weights are assumptions. Use the ranking to shortlist sites and routes; then check the shortlist against the operator's own impression data before a contract is signed.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Change the fast-food weights to 0.6 footfall and 0.2 businesses. How many of the top ten shelters change?
2. Remove the 1000 m features. Does the spatial-CV error rise or fall, and why?
3. Replace the sum of route scores with the mean, and the mean with the maximum. Which would a media buyer prefer, and for which advertiser?
4. Add the weekend count as a second target. Which predictors change importance?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** Not computed in the chapter. Note first that 0.15 + 0.6 + 0.2 + 0.1 = 1.05, so lower income + population to 0.10 or rescale. With footfall at 0.6 the fast-food score follows the predicted count closely, so the top ten moves towards the busiest CBD spine and transport hubs (Town Hall, Central, Wynyard) and away from shelters ranked high only for fast-food density. Count how many of the ten change; if most change, the ranking depends on the weights more than on the data, which a client should be told.

**2.** Not computed in the chapter. The 1000 m features describe the district, which neighbouring sites share almost entirely, so they help random folds (interpolation between near-twins) more than spatial folds. Under spatial CV the error is likely to change little, because the importance ranking is led by 100 m and 500 m features; it may even fall slightly if the 1000 m means are mostly noise near the City boundary, where OpenStreetMap is cut off. Whichever way it moves, compare the change with the fold-to-fold spread before calling it real.

**3.** The sum ranks routes by length (reach), the mean by the average audience per location (quality), and the maximum by the single best stop. A buyer wanting broad reach at low cost per person, typically fast food, might accept the sum but should see length beside it; financial services and education, which target an audience, want the mean; the maximum is useful for choosing one site, not a route, because one good stop says nothing about the other forty.

**4.** Not computed in the chapter. Expect predictors tied to work to lose importance on weekends (job density, floor-space ratio, office building volume), and those tied to leisure and shopping to gain (points of interest, fast food, night-time light around Haymarket, Darling Harbour and the shopping streets). If the weekend model is fitted on the same sites, compare permutation importance on the held-out sites for both targets, side by side.
:::
